### Question 1

Think of each ounce as a little 30 mL cup. If you line up 8 of those little cups, you have 8 x 30 = 240 mL of water. We switch from ounces to milliliters because that is the 'ruler' nurses use to measure all fluids the same way.

### Question 2

'Milli' is a math word that means one-thousandth, like a millimeter is a tiny slice of a meter. So it takes 1000 of the tiny milliliters to fill up one big liter, the same way it takes 1000 grams to make one kilogram.

### Question 3

Water is special: about one gram of it takes up one milliliter of space, and pee is almost all water. So if the diaper got 45 grams heavier, that heaviness came from about 45 mL of pee soaking in. We weigh it because you cannot pour a diaper into a measuring cup.

### Question 4

Imagine a bathtub: water pouring in is intake, water draining out is output. Here 1500 poured in but 1900 drained out, so the tub lost 400 mL. The minus sign is just a flag that says 'more went out than came in.'

### Question 5

A cup full of ice chips is really part ice and part air gaps. When it melts, the ice collapses into a puddle only about half as big. So 200 mL of chips gives your body about 100 mL of real water.

### Question 6

Output is everything that leaves the body, not just the pee. So you add up the pee (1200), the throw-up (150), and the fluid from the wound tube (80) to get 1430 mL total. Forgetting any one of them would make it look like the patient lost less than they really did.

### Question 7

For each person, subtract what went out from what came in. Patient A kept 500 mL extra (a plus), while Patient B lost 500 mL (a minus). They are mirror images, and the one with the plus is Patient A.

### Question 8

Add up every drink and every bag: 240 juice + 180 tea + 500 IV + 50 medicine fluid. That comes to 970 mL. The little 50 mL of medicine fluid is easy to forget, but it still went into the body, so it counts.

### Question 9

Line up all the pee amounts (350, 400, 300) and add the watery stool (200), because watery stool is really fluid leaving the body. Together that is 1250 mL. Only the liquid kind counts, not solid stool.

### Question 10

To find the per-hour amount, share the 200 mL evenly across the 8 hours: 200 / 8 = 25 mL each hour. Nurses check this against a rule of thumb of about 30 mL every hour. Since 25 is under 30, this patient is making a little less urine than we want to see.

### Question 11

Turn the cups into mL first: 24 ounces x 30 = 720 mL, plus the 1000 mL bag makes 1720 mL in. Out is 1400 pee + 250 drain = 1650 mL. In minus out is 1720 - 1650 = a small plus of 70 mL.

### Question 12

To be fair to big and small people, we spread the pee out over the hours and over each kilogram of body weight. So 480 mL split across 8 hours and 60 kg comes out to 1 mL for each kilogram each hour, which is a healthy amount.
